hops.title: True Blue and the visual neurons that once reached for the spinal cord
hops.text: In 1982, Brent Stanfield, Dennis O'Leary and C. Fricks were mapping which cortical neurons send axons down the pyramidal tract toward the spinal cord. They injected a fluorescent tracer called True Blue where that tract crosses in the brainstem. In rats in their first week of life, labeled neurons turned up across nearly the whole neocortex, visual cortex included. In adult rats, the same injection labels none there. So did the young visual neurons die? The team injected in week one and looked again at week four. The blue cells were still sitting in visual cortex. They had lived and dropped only the branch headed for the spinal cord.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A white laboratory rat sitting on a wooden bench beside a cobalt-blue glass vial in daylight.
image.caption: Young rat visual neurons send a branch toward the spinal cord, then drop the branch and keep living.

hops.title: Why eye doctors patch a child's stronger eye
hops.text: When amblyopia affects one eye in childhood, the brain comes to rely on the stronger eye while vision in the weaker eye falls behind. After addressing any underlying vision problem, one clinician-directed treatment patches the stronger eye so the brain uses the weaker one. In 1993, Antonella Antonini and Michael Stryker closed one eye in kittens during the critical period and traced single thalamic axon arbors in visual cortex. Branches relaying the deprived eye's input withdrew rapidly. A 2003 trial of 189 children under seven with moderate amblyopia found that shorter and longer daily patching schedules, each with close-up tasks, gave similar vision gains at four months.

sources.citation: Repka et al. (Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group), Arch. Ophthalmol. 121:603-611 (2003)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A smiling young child wearing a patterned cloth eye patch over one eye, assembling a wooden puzzle at a sunny table.
image.caption: Patching makes the brain use the weaker eye; in kittens, thalamic axon branches carrying deprived-eye input withdraw in cortex.

hops.title: Moths that remember what they learned as caterpillars
hops.text: A common picture is that metamorphosis wipes a caterpillar's nervous system clean. In 2008, Georgetown biologists tested whether a learned odor aversion survives metamorphosis. They paired ethyl acetate with a mild electric shock in late-stage tobacco hornworms; 78 percent then avoided the odor in a Y-shaped choice apparatus. About a month later, 77 percent of adult moths still avoided it. In a separate carryover test, scrubbing trained caterpillars' pupal cases with a soft brush and distilled water did not erase the aversion. Caterpillars trained earlier, as third instars, showed no clear preference as adults. That fits early-born fly gamma neurons pruning larval branches, though this study did not test it.

sources.citation: Blackiston, Silva Casey & Weiss, PLoS ONE 3:e1736 (2008)

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A green tobacco hornworm caterpillar and an adult hawkmoth beside a clear Y-shaped tunnel on a sunny greenhouse bench.
image.caption: Metamorphosis does not wipe the slate: moths keep an odor lesson learned late in caterpillar life.

audio.title: Toddlers, ground squirrels and moths with good memories
audio.transcript:
When you hear that a neuron cuts away its own branches and stays alive, it can sound like damage. Here are three true stories where cutting back or rebuilding sits alongside normal life: falling synapse density in a growing human brain, retracting dendrites in a hibernating squirrel, and a moth that still avoids a smell it learned as a caterpillar.

First, whose frontal cortex packs more synapses into the same tiny volume of tissue, a toddler's or a college student's? You might guess the college student. In nineteen seventy-nine, the pediatric neurologist Peter Huttenlocher counted synapses in electron micrographs from twenty-one human brains, from newborns to ninety-year-olds. The peak was not in college. It was between ages one and two. In the patch of frontal cortex he sampled, synaptic density at that peak was roughly fifty percent above the adult average. Between ages two and sixteen, the density fell back toward the adult level. Later work by Huttenlocher and Dabholkar, in nineteen ninety-seven, showed that different regions run on different clocks. Auditory cortex peaks around three months and finishes its net trimming by age twelve. Prefrontal cortex peaks after fifteen months and keeps trimming into midadolescence. Growing up, it turns out, involves losing connections as well as making them.

Second, some mammals pull their branches in and grow them back on a schedule. Hibernating ground squirrels spend a week or more at a time with brain temperatures near freezing. In two thousand six, Christina von der Ohe and colleagues at Stanford looked closely at neurons in the squirrel hippocampus, cortex and thalamus. As the animals cooled into torpor, their neurons pulled back their dendrites and lost spines, and the cell bodies shrank, and the colder the animal got, the more they retracted. As the squirrels warmed back up, spine density rebounded and most of the recovery took place within about two hours. Twelve hours after arousal, the colder and warmer groups showed no significant differences in cell body size, dendritic branching or spine density across the neurons studied. This is dendrites rather than axons, but it shows how readily living neurons can pull their branches in and grow them back.

Finally, a common picture is that metamorphosis wipes a caterpillar's nervous system clean. In two thousand eight, biologists at Georgetown put that to the test with tobacco hornworm caterpillars. They trained late-stage, fifth-instar caterpillars to avoid the smell of ethyl acetate, pairing the smell with a mild electric shock, and in a Y-shaped choice apparatus seventy-eight percent steered clear. After four to five weeks as pupae, the moths emerged, and three days later seventy-seven percent of the adults still chose the unscented arm. In a separate test, the aversion held even when the researchers scrubbed the pupal cases with a soft brush and distilled water. Caterpillars trained earlier, at third instar, still avoided the odor two molts later, eighty-one percent of them, but as adults that group showed no clear preference. That timing fits what you saw in fly mushroom bodies, where early-born gamma neurons prune their larval branches during metamorphosis, although the moth study did not test that directly. Either way, a moth can come out of metamorphosis still avoiding a smell it learned to dislike as a caterpillar.
